video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Three Ways to Get Big Flavor with Less Meat: Dan Dan Mien, Braised Collards, Anchovy-Powered Pasta
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: This ATK segment demonstrates how to extract deep flavor from a small amount of meat across three dishes. It starts with a Dan Dan Mien where ground pork is browned in a thin smear for maximum surface contact, then builds a concentrated chili-oil-based sauce with Sichuan aromatics and a dried-yacai accent. A second showcase braises ham hocks to create a lush pot liquor for braised collard greens, emphasizing long, gentle extraction of flavor and collagen. The third demonstrates a fast, high-umami pasta sauce built around anchovies, plus a parsley-basil pesto that doubles as an umami booster, finished with pasta water to emulsify and lightly coat angel hair. Throughout, the host highlights techniques for flavorful results from limited meat, including browning, tension between texture and flavor, layering of aromatics, and science-backed umami boosters.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Pasta Water Mastery: Emulsifying Sauces and Special Techniques with Lan Lam
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: In this Techniquely episode with Lan Lam, viewers learn practical ways to use pasta cooking water to shape and finish sauces. The host demonstrates finishing sauce by allowing briefly cooked pasta to mingle with its sauce, then reintroducing reserve pasta water to rehydrate and emulsify, yielding a cohesive, glossy texture. He explores a classic Cacio e Pepe approach that uses toasted peppercorns, finely ground Pecorino Romano, and hot water to create a velvety emulsion, while also showcasing an oil-based tuna and capers sauce built through starch-rich cooking water and controlled heat to keep fats emulsified. The video emphasizes timing, texture cues (sheen vs. shininess), and temperature control to avoid over-softening pasta, with side notes on jarred sauce evaluation and other sauce-building ideas. Overall, it provides a practical, evidence-backed framework for using pasta water to adjust sauce consistency and mouthfeel across different sauce types.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Techniquely: Super Crunchy Buttermilk Fried Chicken — trim, brine, dredge + batter, fry at 340°F
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: America’s Test Kitchen’s Techniquely episode walks through a method to achieve an exceptionally crispy, craggy fried chicken crust by pairing a dredge with a buttermilk-based batter, preceded by careful trimming, strategic breast-halving for even cooking, and a flexible brining step. The host trims fat and extra skin, cuts breasts on a diagonal for even pieces, and brines the chicken with salt (plus optional sugar, garlic powder, and cayenne) for flavor and juiciness. The coating uses a flour-cornstarch base with baking powder, seasoned to echo the brine, plus a viscous buttermilk batter. Frying is conducted at 340°F in two batches with safety-minded techniques (low dipping height, singleton hands for handling batter, and per-piece temperature checks). The video emphasizes carryover cooking, advising pulling darker meat at 160°F and breasts at 140°F to finish in residual heat, resulting in juicy meat and a crust that stays intact without dragging or greasing-up. The host also notes practical workflow tips (pan choice for dredge, over‑shooting heat for recovery, and avoiding a doughy undercoat) and points viewers to the ATK app for the full recipe and Cook Mode guidance.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Grilling with Fire: Flare-Ups, Fat Control, and Flambé Flavor
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: This Techniquely episode from America's Test Kitchen explores how fire shapes flavor across grilling, indoor flame techniques, and even cocktails. It covers prepping chicken thighs with a gochujang-based paste, cooking on a two-zone grill to control flare-ups, and finishing on the hot side for crisp skin and smoky notes. The segment then transitions to indoors, explaining wok hei-style flavor and the flambé technique, illustrated with a Calvados-enhanced pork chop dish, safety steps, and how flame-driven Maillard browning contributes depth to sauces. The video concludes with practical cocktail flame tips and an orange-garnish demonstration, emphasizing subtlety and safety when using fire to tweak flavor.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Mini Peanut Praline Chocolate Pies: Crust, Praline, and Namelaka
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: Lan Lam guides viewers through a three-in-one holiday dessert: mini peanut praline chocolate pies with a paper-thin, buttery crust, a roast-praline layer, and a silky Namelaka chocolate cream. The episode emphasizes beginner-friendly technique: a crust made in a food processor with extra water for sufficient gluten development, a dough rolled to about 1/8 inch thickness and baked in muffin cups to form shells, a two-stage bake to keep the shells flat, and a caramel-praline component ground to a dust and mixed with peanut butter. The Namelaka is built from gelatin-softened milk and melted chocolate, cooled to room temperature, then thickened with cream and piped into the shells. The host also shares practical hacks (Saint Honor piping with a simple plastic bag), finish with flaky salt, and storage guidelines, illustrating how each component can be used separately in other desserts.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: 3 Salting Methods for Better-Tasting Meats
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: This video from America's Test Kitchen presents a practical, evidence-based look at three salt-application approaches for meat and fish: brining (salting in a saltwater solution), dry brining (salting directly on the surface and letting salt disperse into the meat), and seasoning (salting during cooking). It details how salt affects protein structure and water retention, provides specific brine concentrations and timing guidelines for different proteins, demonstrates a quick salmon brine, and shows poultry preparation that yields crispy skin through overnight air-drying. It also covers salt types and density differences, and ends with general seasoning rules, a three-finger technique for even distribution, and a reverse-sear pork demonstration, all aimed at helping cooks decide when and how to apply salt based on product size, timing, and space available.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: One-Hour Broiled Chicken Prep: Trimming, Spatchcocking, and Carving with Lan Lam (ATK Techniquely)
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: In this ATK Techniquely episode, Lan Lam demonstrates comprehensive prep techniques for whole chicken and its parts to streamline pan-searing/broiling and to improve cook evenness and presentation. The video covers cavity inspection and trimming, choosing between scissors and knife for trimming, backbone removal and spatchcocking, wing-tucking and leg-tying with twine, oiling and seasoning inside and out, and a skillet-first broil finish. It then walks through splitting and trimming bone-in and boneless breasts, trimming and deboning thighs, and preparing drumsticks, followed by resting, carving, and finishing with a simple pan sauce from the roasted juices. The lesson emphasizes practical knife work, fat management, and portioning cuts for even cooking, with tips on tool choice and rest-time gains in texture and flavor.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Tangzhong Method for Fluffy Dinner Rolls and Enriched Breads
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: This video explains the tangzhong (water roux) technique and demonstrates its impact on producing ultra-fluffy, tender dinner rolls and other fine-crumb breads. Lan Lam explains the science behind bread structure—gluten formation from flour proteins and starch interactions—then shows how cooking a portion of flour and water into a tangzhong alters hydration and crumb. The host details practical usage: using 5–10% of flour for the tangzhong, heating methods, cooling considerations to avoid killing yeast, and incorporating the mixture into dough. Additional segments cover shaping to build internal structure, pan-based rising to encourage height, and applying tangzhong to challah dough to maintain firmness. The video also discusses slowing staling, with guidance on which bread types are best suited to tangzhong and how it affects shelf life.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Resting Meat: Carryover Cooking, Juices, and Rest Timings
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: The video explains that resting meat after cooking is not idle but a crucial step because carryover cooking continues after removal from heat. It illuminates how a hotter surface compared with the interior drives a continued rise in the center, influenced by oven temperature and the size of the piece. Higher cooking temperatures and larger cuts can justify longer rests, while the surface-to-center temperature differential explains why finished doneness shifts during resting. A practical demonstration compares rested versus immediately sliced meat, showing reduced juice loss and improved juiciness—especially for chicken and pork—when rested. The host also contrasts methods such as searing followed by resting versus sous vide, noting that with a uniform water-bath cook there is little carryover and texture can differ. General resting guidelines are provided (turkey 30–45 minutes; roasts 15–20 minutes; steaks, chops, and chicken 5–10 minutes), along with caveats for when not to rest (e.g., tuna to preserve crust and a raw interior, or when a roast is overcooked and slicing helps the surface). The takeaway is a practical framework: use rest time to finish carryover cooking, retain juices, and plan service around the meat’s size, temperature, and cooking method.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Bartender Techniques for Better Cocktails: Stirring, Shaking, Temperature, and Ice
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: This video breaks down practical bartending techniques into four core areas that influence cocktail quality: stirring, shaking, precise ingredient measurement, and temperature management through glassware and ice. Lan Lam demonstrates a stirred drink (the Little Bologna) to illustrate how generous ice, smooth bar-spoon motion, and proper dilution chill and texture the cocktail; then pivots to shaking with a Sidecar to show aggressive, equipment-driven mixing, straining choices, and aroma effects. The segment on measurement emphasizes reliable pouring and the use of dropper bottles or measuring spoons to achieve balance across spirits, citrus, sweeteners, and bitters. Temperature discussion covers pre-chilled glassware, how to quickly chill a glass, and why serving at the right temperature matters for aroma and perceived sweetness. Finally, the video highlights ice quality—dry, appropriately sized cubes for stirring or shaking, and the impact of wet ice on dilution—along with visual tests of glass temperature and the concept of ‘fridge-door’ cocktails as a prep strategy. Throughout, it anchors tips to the book Cocktails Illustrated and practical demonstrations of recipes like Little Bologna and Sidecars, illustrating how to apply these techniques at home with real tools and measurements.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: The Formula to Great Fried Rice with Any Ingredients
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: America's Test Kitchen presents a practical, universal approach to fried rice, codifying a core formula that works with a wide range of ingredients and styles. The video walks through rice preparation (emphasizing the use of stale rice for optimal grain separation, with alternatives for fresh rice and brown rice), a flexible mix-ins plan (eggs plus any proteins and vegetables), and a step-by-step cooking order using a wok. Key techniques include preheating a carbon steel wok, cooking ingredients sequentially to maintain texture and flavor, using fats to carry aromatics, salting at strategic moments, and finishing with optional additions like water to loosen stubborn rice clumps. The host demonstrates practical pacing, mise en place, and seasoning strategy, concluding with garnishes and a reminder that the rice-to-mix-ins ratio should emphasize the grain for the signature fried-rice texture.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Pete Bread (Pon Dulce) Made by Hand: Enriched Dough from Start to Finish
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: In this America’s Test Kitchen video, Artisan Brian Ford demonstrates making Pete bread—a silky, buttery, enriched loaf referenced from Pon Dulce Pon Dulce—entirely by hand and compares it to a mixer approach. The hosts cover weighing ingredients (vs. volume), choosing yeast (fresh vs. instant/dry) with a quick conversion, and managing hydration for enriched dough by reserving water and gradually adding fats. The demonstration then shifts from mixer to hand kneading, showing how to incorporate butter while developing gluten, followed by a 5-minute rest, shaping into rounds and a pan loaf, and two proofing stages. The bake is done at 375°F with an egg wash, and doneness is discussed via color and internal temperature around 200°F. The video includes tasting and sandwich-building ideas to illustrate the bread’s tender, springy crumb. Throughout, the dialog emphasizes technique over guesswork, with practical tips on dough texture, timing, and shaping for a well-formed loaf.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Three Practical Raw-Fish Techniques from ATK: Tuna Bowl with Blanching, Ceviche (Leche de Tigre), and Gravlax
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: America’s Test Kitchen’s Techniquely episode demonstrates three accessible raw-fish preparations anchored in careful sourcing and hands-on technique: a tuna bowl that uses hot-water blanching to firm the exterior and a flavorful marinade; a ceviche-style preparation with leche de tigre and a lime-based emulsion that gently “cooks” the fish through acid; and a gravlax-style salmon cure that relies on salt, sugar, and dill over several days. The video emphasizes starting with properly handled fish (often frozen and defrosted under controlled conditions), precise knife work for clean cuts, marination timing to balance flavor and texture, and practical plating and garnishing ideas. Safety notes cover parasite considerations, the relative risks of raw fish for certain populations, and the distinction between acid- versus heat-induced changes in fish proteins.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Beautiful, Flavorful Cookies: Dump-and-Stir Dough, Log Shaping, and Finishes
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: Lan Lam walks through a practical, flavor-forward approach to cookies built on a simple dump-and-stir dough, two reliable log-shaping methods to produce uniform, sliceable cookies, and flexible finishing options including fruit dust, nuts, and chocolate. The lesson emphasizes flavor versatility (vanilla as a base plus citrus spice, dried fruit, and nuts), shaping techniques that ensure even diameter for uniform cookies, chilling and slicing mechanics, and baking cues. Finishes cover both melted and tempered chocolate (with a faux-tempering walkthrough attributed to Andrea Giri) and decorative toppings like freeze-dried fruit dust to create color and pattern. Throughout, Lan shares several flavor pairings (almond with sour cherries; pistachio with apricot; peppermint mocha mosaic) and notes that full recipes are available on cooksillustrated.com, with links in the description.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: ATK Pancakes: Easy Pancakes and Cottage Cheese High-Protein Pancakes — Batter Tech, Pan Method, and Creative Toppings
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: This ATK episode presents two pancake variations with parallel techniques aimed at reliability and texture: a classic Easy Pancakes batter and a High-Protein Cottage Cheese Pancakes batter. The instructor walks through constructing the batters from dry and wet components, explains leaveners and rest time to encourage height, demonstrates heat management on a skillet or griddle, and details testing, scooping, and flipping to achieve tall, evenly browned pancakes. The cottage cheese version shows how to blend ingredients to reduce lumps, harness the cheese’s moisture for spread, and cook on a controllable griddle for multiple pancakes at once. The video closes with topping ideas, including an orange almond compound butter and a yogurt–jam combination, and ends with tasting notes and encouragement to try the tips across recipes.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Baking Soda in Ground Meat: Juicier, Browner Beef and Turkey Burgers (Chili and Skillet Turkey Burgers)
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: The video demonstrates a simple, evidence-backed technique: treating ground meat with a small amount of baking soda dissolved in water to keep it juicy, tender, and better browned. Through beef chili and turkey burgers, the host explains dosing per pound, dispersal methods to avoid clumps, and the science behind why the alkaline treatment changes protein interactions to retain moisture and foster browning. The beef chili example shows a two-pound batch with specific soda and salt amounts, aromatics, and a long, gentle oven braise to finish the dish, while the turkey burgers emphasize a cold-start method with minimal handling and a binder-rich mix for a juicy patty. The segment ends with tasting and a takeaway that the baking soda trick can improve any ground-meat recipe.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Heel-of-the-knife mince: shallots and garlic with precise control
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: Lan Lam demonstrates an alternative to traditional shallot mincing by using the heel of a non-bolster knife to make vertical cuts first, enabling tighter spacing and improved control since the distance between the back of the blade and the wrist is smaller. This method is contrasted with the conventional horizontal-then-vertical approach and is extended to garlic, where she shows skipping horizontal cuts and completing the mince with a 90-degree clove flip and a final pass. The video emphasizes knife anatomy (the bolster) and a gentle rocking motion to guide the blade straight down, yielding uniform pieces suitable for vinaigrettes and pan sauces. The tips focus on precision, blade alignment, and practice, with encouragement to try the technique on a couple of shallots before applying it in recipes.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Marinating Fundamentals: Base, Salt, Surface Area, and Browning
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: Lan Lam outlines the core structure of marinades, emphasizing a water-based base and salt as must-haves, with oil, sugar, and flavorings as optional add-ons. Using Dan Souza’s skillet chicken fajitas as an example, she walks through how base liquid and salt enable even flavor and juiciness, how to maximize surface contact by thinning or pounding meat, and how to time and cook marinated meat for a browned exterior and juicy interior. The video also covers safe reuse of marinade (boil to kill microbes) and practical guidelines for customizing marinades while keeping the core ratios intact. Practical steps include dry-patting before cooking, searing in a smoking-hot pan, finishing in a low-heat oven, resting the meat, and slicing across the grain to finish with flavorful pan juices.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Stop Butter Basting Meat, Do This Instead | Techniquely with Lan Lam
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: Lan Lam reframes butter basting as not universally required for home cooking and walks through practical, timing-conscious alternatives across proteins. The video contrasts traditional basting with more efficient methods, using steak as the primary example, and then extends the approach to pan sauces for chicken and flaky fish. By focusing on heat management, browning, and building flavor through fond-based sauces (instead of relying on continuous basting), the episode demonstrates how to achieve sear, depth of flavor, and moisture with minimal fuss. The demonstrations—steak without aggressive basting, a brown-butter finish, skillet-roasted chicken, and Steve Dunn’s fish-baste method—are tied together with guidance on when baste is advantageous (notably for delicate fish) and when it’s safer to skip it while still delivering a robust, flavorful result.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Microwave Power, Timing, and Garnish Techniques: Beyond Reheat
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: America's Test Kitchen's Techniquely episode explains how microwaves heat food, dispels common myths, and demonstrates practical techniques to maximize results: using power level (on/off cycles) for even heating; butter softening, quick vegetable prep, and reheating frozen soup; plus microwave-based garnishes and finishing touches such as fried capers, shallots, frico crisps, orange almond compound butter, and caramel sauce. The transcript presents core concepts of microwave operation, the surface-localized heating of foods, and safe handling while showing actionable steps for everyday cooking.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Essential Knife Skills: Grip, Slice, Dice, Mince — with Lan Lam
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: Lan Lam demonstrates core knife skills in a practical kitchen context, beginning with a story about brunoise to motivate precision and efficiency. He emphasizes a sharp chef’s knife, a pinch grip, and ergonomic alignment from shoulder to blade; he explains safe offhand positioning and fingertip protection. The lesson covers slicing (including diagonal push cuts and pull cuts), dicing (including decisions about edge squaring versus waste), and mincing (with a focus on delicate herbs). He also shows garlic technique to maximize flavor, and closes with a real-world application through Japchae, illustrating how these skills translate to efficient, less-wasteful cooking in the home kitchen. The video blends technique demonstrations with commentary on form, control, and safety, inviting viewer practice and engagement.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Crispy Fried Cutlets: SBP Variations, Crumbs, and Frying Techniques
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: This Techniquely episode outlines the standard breading procedure (SBP) for crispy fried cutlets and dives into practical variations used across tonkatsu, schnitzel, and chicken parmigiana. It breaks down the three-part coating (flour, egg wash, breadcrumbs), explains how crumb size, type, and seasonings affect texture and flavor, and presents tweaks to boost crust integrity (Parmesan in crumbs for water resistance, egg-wash adjustments, batter-leaning approaches). The host then covers frying strategies tailored to meat thickness (shallow frying with a 2/3 oil depth, straight-sided pans), how to manage batter adhesion with a dry hand/wet hand method, and techniques to prevent crust collapse or cupping (perforating fat/silver skin, resting cuts on their side). The episode also shares methods for easier execution for those who fry infrequently, crumb-pressing tips, and finishing touches for each dish (schnitzel, tonkatsu, chicken parmesan) followed by a recap of how SBP can vary to distinguish similar fried dishes while maintaining crisp texture.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Crispy Potatoes Without Deep Frying: Three No-Fry Techniques from Techniquely with Lan Lam
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: This video explains the science of achieving crispy potatoes without deep frying and demonstrates three no-fry methods. Lan Lam contextualizes the idea that crispness comes from a dry starch network formed when water is driven off and heat and oil render that network into a browned, crunchy exterior. The three methods shown are: roasted smashed potatoes (steam-roasted, then smashed for maximum surface contact and browning), home fries pre-treated with an alkaline boil (baking soda in water to rough up exterior before roasting with aromatics), and oven fries coated with a cornstarch slurry (microwave-thickened slurry to build a protective shell, then steamed and browned). Each method emphasizes not cooking and crisping simultaneously, but sequencing steam, starch development, and browning to achieve a crispy, fluffy interior without deep frying.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Pâte à Choux: The All-Purpose Dough for Profiteroles, Gougères, and Gnocchi
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: This video presents pâte à choux as a universal, versatile dough that can be used for both sweet and savory dishes. The host walks through the classic double-cooking method: starting the paste on the stovetop, then binding it with eggs (emphasizing one-at-a-time addition and a food processor option to vent steam), and finally baking to produce crisp, hollow puffs. The demonstration covers practical technique for piping and shaping, plus several ready-to-plate variations: sweet profiteroles filled with ice cream and topped with chocolate, savory gougères with cayenne and Gruyère, and a gnocchi alla parisienne made from choux dough. Throughout, the video emphasizes steam-leavening (no commercial leaveners) and time/temperature control to achieve lift and crisp shells, with tips on batching, storing, and finishing sauces and fillings. All recipes and techniques are presented as ways to leverage one dough for multiple dishes.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: The Best Way to Cook Shrimp
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: This ATK Techniquely episode presents a masterclass on cooking shrimp with attention to texture, moisture, and browning. The host contrasts frozen vs. fresh shrimp, explains how salting and moisture management affect tenderness, and demonstrates a cold-start, high-heat sear to achieve even browning without overcooking. It then blends in flavor-building steps: a quick toast of a spice mix, a finish with lime and cilantro, and practical variations such as sous-vide poaching and a brined shrimp cocktail approach with accompanying sauce ideas. Throughout, the emphasis is on controlling moisture, heat, and timing to keep shrimp tender, juicy, and flavorful rather than dry or rubbery.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Bare-Simmer Pasta and Crispy Gnocchi: Fresh Noodles, Sesame Sauce, and Pan-Fried Gnocchi Techniques
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: This instructional video from America's Test Kitchen reconsiders common pasta directions by demonstrating a bare-simmer approach to fresh noodles and noodle-adjacent products (such as Liang mian) to preserve texture and absorption. It covers sauce-building with sesame paste (and substitute options), emulsified dressings, and minimal rinsing to maintain chew and surface quality. A substantial portion is devoted to shelf-stable gnocchi, prepared with a cold pan start, generous oil, and a quick vegetable-tinish sauce finish. The segment ends with a concise comparison of fresh versus dried pasta, including how to treat fresh nests and how to use starchy pasta water to finish sauces. Throughout, practical tips, substitutions, and serving ideas (toppings, add-ins, and storage considerations) are offered as a unified approach to quick, flavorful noodle-centered dishes.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Roast Two Chickens at Once: Hot-Pan Technique, Off-Oven Finish, and Schmaltz/Stock
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: This ATK Techniquely episode demonstrates roasting two roughly 4-lb chickens in one batch using a preheated roasting pan and a finishing phase powered by residual oven heat. The host trims fat and skin to render cracklings, slides in slits to drain juices, seasons and trusses the birds, and roasts them on a hot pan without a rack. The technique emphasizes timing so the breast reaches 160–165°F while the thighs reach doneness via residual heat. After resting, the video shows carving both birds efficiently, collecting pan drippings to make stock, schmaltz, and gribenes, and then re-heating leftovers with steam and a brief skillet finish. It packs practical, repeatable steps for weeknight meals and emphasizes using the carcass remnants for flavorful stock and fat. There are also tips on utilizing pan drippings for dressings and flavoring other dishes.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Sous Vide Cooking: Essentials for Home Cooks
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: America’s Test Kitchen’s Techniquely overview explains sous vide basics for home cooks, clarifying why the technique gained restaurant fame and how it translates to everyday cooking. It covers essential equipment (immersion circulator, containers, lids), temperature and timing guidelines (target around 130°F for medium-rare steak, with 125°F internal target and carryover), practical bagging strategies (Ziploc bags with air removed via water displacement, optional vacuum sealer), flavoring ideas (salt timing, thyme in the bag, oil to distribute aromatics, safe use of garlic powder), finishing techniques (sear after bath for Maillard crust, pan sauce made from bag juices), and key safety and workflow tips (avoid overlong baths, don’t overcrowd the bath, keep air out of bags). The video also demonstrates a dramatic example: 72-hour short rib finished with a blowtorch, illustrating sous vide’s texture and uniformity potential, and points viewers toward further recipes and guidance such as Sous Vide for Everybody.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Rethinking Pasta: Emulsified Sauces, Cold Starts, and Water-Saving Techniques
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: This America's Test Kitchen Techniquely episode examines alternatives to the classic pasta boil in a large pot of salted water. Lan Lam tests both a traditional high-water approach and a reduced-water method that leverages starch-rich pasta water to emulsify sauces, render fats, and finish dishes with richness without greasiness. The video also explores a cold-start technique to conserve water and energy, a Gricia-style preparation with guanciale to build flavor, and an egg-and-cheese finish that uses pasta starch as the sauce’s thickener. Through practical tips on doneness testing, saving pasta water, and choosing methods based on pasta shape and sauce body, the host invites experimentation beyond conventional rules.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Oven Rack Placement, Preheating, and Convection: Techniques from Techniquely with Lan Lam
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: America’s Test Kitchen’s Techniquely episode with Lan Lam explains common oven mistakes and how to fix them by focusing on rack placement, full preheating, and heat sources. The video demonstrates practical setups for thin-crust pizza on a stone with the rack close to the broiler, a bottom-rack strategy for cast-iron pan pizzas, and broiled zucchini, then discusses convection’s effects on multiple racks, browning, and timing, culminating in three core takeaways: adjust the rack, let the oven fully heat, and tailor convection with notes for future tweaks.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Steam-First Reverse Sear for Brussels Sprouts, Cabbage, and Fennel
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: The video demonstrates a vegetable reverse-sear workflow adapted from meat cookery: trim and shape Brussels sprouts, cabbage, and fennel into flat, uniform pieces; cook the interior with steam before exposing the surface to high heat for browning. The prep emphasizes flat sides and even sizing to maximize pan contact, while the technique employs water-based steaming (with optional brine) to deliver heat to interior portions. After steaming, the lid/foil is removed to allow Maillard browning, aided by oil to improve heat transfer. The segment concludes with plating ideas (maple vinaigrette, smoked almonds, sesame seeds, scallions) and notes on applying this method to other vegetables like cauliflower and broccoli.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: The Only Scrambled Eggs Recipe You'll Ever Need: Early Salt, Pan Control, and Finishing Techniques
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: In this ATK Techniquely episode hosted by Lan Lam, the video teaches a practical approach to scrambled eggs aimed at delivering tender, custardy texture tailored to the eater. The host covers portioning per person, salting the eggs in advance to season and modify protein structure, and the optional use of dairy or water to influence richness and tenderness. A focused set of equipment choices—an appropriately sized 8-inch nonstick skillet, a rubber spatula, and a lid—drives the technique, along with strategic heat management and constant stirring to control doneness. The segment concludes with flexible garnishes (such as chili crisp, pesto, furikake, harissa) and serving ideas, plus pointers to the ATK app for the recipe. The lesson emphasizes adapting the method to personal taste while providing concrete measurements, timing cues, and texture indicators to prevent overcooking.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Fast and Fresh Veg Sides: Blanching, Salt-Bruising, and Pan-Steaming with Beurre Monte Finish
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: In this ATK segment, Lan Lam demonstrates a restaurant-inspired approach to keeping vegetables vibrant and fast on the plate by rethinking prep rather than reinventing cooking. The lesson walks through blanching vegetables to near doneness and shocking them in an ice bath to preserve texture and flavor, followed by salt-bruising (yamitsuki-inspired) cabbage to concentrate sweetness. It then shows a pan-steaming technique for broccoli/broccolini using a small amount of water and a lid to generate steam, finishing florets with a butter-based beurre monte sauce laced with lemon zest, thyme, shallot, and pepper. The video also covers meal-prep strategies for blanching ahead, reheating methods, and practical salt ratios for flavorful, quickly served veg alongside proteins.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Overcooking Vegetables On Purpose: Techniques for Creamy, Tender Veg (Techniquely with Lan Lam)
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: This America's Test Kitchen Techniquely episode with Lan Lam reframes overcooking from a dietary hazard to a deliberate technique for texture and flavor. The video blends a short science primer on plant cell structure with practical demonstrations that push vegetables beyond their standard crispness: eggplant is slow-roasted to dissolve cell-wall components into a creamy sauce, green beans are braised to absorb flavor, and broccoli is simmered into a rich soup that preserves color and nutty notes. Across segments—Walk Away Ratatouille, Mediterranean Braised Green Beans, and broccoli-cheese soup—the host shows how manipulating hemicellulose, pectin, and chlorophyll through time, pH, and temperature can transform vegetables into luxurious textures and concentrated flavors, while still honoring their identity as vegetables. The episode also highlights finishing touches (vinaigars, parsley, spinach wilt, cheese blends) and emphasizes that overcooking can be a thoughtful tool rather than a flaw.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Butter-Washed Bourbon: Grated Butter Infusion and Two Flavor Outputs
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: The video demonstrates a butter-based fat-wash technique inspired by bacon-wash, using grated butter to infuse bourbon and extract two products: bourbon-flavored butter and butter-flavored bourbon. The presenter grates two sticks of butter, packs them into a mason jar, pours bourbon (7 oz used in the example), and refrigerates the mixture for 1–2 days before straining through cheesecloth. The resulting infused liquids are then used in cocktails (notably Manhattan and Old Fashioned) and in a fall-inspired recipe (Autumn in New England) featuring sage, maple syrup, apple cider, and cider vinegar. The clip also suggests uses for the butter (hot honey as a compound butter, buttercream for cupcakes, or spreading on toast) and notes storage timelines for both the butter and the spirit, with a nod to Cook’s Illustrated as the source of the technique. The content addresses optional spirit substitutions (rye, rum, tequila) and invites viewer engagement in the comments.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Maximizing Spice Flavor: Layering Whole and Ground Spices with Time-Release Aromatics in Kima
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: This Techniquely episode analyzes why when and how you add spices changes flavor, using a Kima (ground beef curry) as a through-line. Lan Lam explains that spices are not a single flavor but a blend of aromatic compounds with different volatilities, many of which are drawn out by heating. The video visualizes how aroma components separate in solution, contrasts whole versus ground spices in terms of surface area and release, and demonstrates a two-stage approach to spice addition: browning aromatics and infusing oil with whole spices for depth, then introducing ground spices later to preserve their more delicate notes. The segment also covers recipe scaling, a curry-blend ensemble analogy, and practical steps (browning onions, sautéing garlic/ginger, simmering tomatoes with yogurt, finishing with peas and cilantro) to achieve a cohesive, deeply flavored finished dish.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Restaurant-Style Green Salads: Emulsified Dressings, Gentle Handling, and Finishing Touches
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: America’s Test Kitchen host Lan Lam demonstrates practical, chef-tested techniques to elevate home green salads to restaurant quality. Key ideas include matching dressing to greens by tenderness and texture, constructing a quick emulsified vinaigrette (mayo, mustard, salt, molasses) with two oils and three additions to maintain emulsion, and dispersing dressing early to avoid uneven coating. The video also covers a thick-dressing method that starts in the bowl, hands-on dressing (with optional gloves) to minimize bruising, and a tasting step to fine-tune dressing balance with salt, pepper, and citrus. In addition to a simple no-recipe salad (arugula, lemon, Pecorino), Lam models finishing touches (lemon zest, cracked pepper) and offers make-ahead toppings such as candied nuts, shaved vegetables using ice-water, and crisp croutons. The transcript references specific tools (mason jar, mandolin, salad spinner) and practical kitchen tactics drawn from professional kitchens, adapted for home cooks.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Pan Color and Reflectivity: How Light vs Dark Surfaces Change Searing, Browning, and Baking Outcomes
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: In this short segment from America's Test Kitchen’s Techniquely, Lan Lam explains how the color and shine of cookware influence cooking results. The host argues that light-colored skillets improve visibility of fond formation for pan sauces and help monitor butter browning, while dark pans alter browning and flavor development. The discussion extends to baking, noting that dark cake pans and muffin tins absorb heat and can affect sides and bottoms, with aluminum sheet pans’ reflectivity also changing browning behavior. The video closes with practical notes on shiny versus matte pans and how appearance can guide cooking times, plus references to Gear Heads and Cook’s Illustrated for further information.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Mastering Frozen Produce in Cooking: Techniques, Texture, and Quick Recipes
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: Lan Lam explains how frozen fruits and vegetables can be leveraged beyond smoothies, emphasizing time savings, broader seasonal access, and texture benefits from freezer-damaged foods. The video contrasts slow vs. rapid freezing, introduces IQF (individually quick freezing) as a texture-preserving technique, and demonstrates practical recipes and methods that use frozen produce in cooked dishes. Key demonstrations include squeezing water from defrosted spinach to reduce binder for Gnudi, cooking with frozen peas for Pasta Piselli, and using frozen cranberries to make a tender relish and to extract berry flavor for iced tea, illustrating how freezing can expand menu options while cutting prep and waste.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Water-Driven Browning: Onion Caramelization, Mushroom Searing, and Chicken Gravy
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: In this Techniquely episode from America’s Test Kitchen, Lan Lam explains how adding water to the cooking surface can actually improve browning by using steam to regulate heat and promote Maillard and caramelization reactions. The transcript introduces two browning modalities—caramelization and Maillard browning—and explains why surface water keeps temperatures near 212°F, which can inhibit browning unless leveraged strategically. The video then demonstrates three water-assisted browning applications: caramelized onions cooked with a lid to trap steam for rapid wilting before browning; sautéed mushrooms that begin with a small amount of oil and a measured amount of water to generate steam and concentrate browning; and a chicken gravy built from browned stock where water extracts sugars and amino acids to support Maillard browning, followed by reduction and roux to finish the sauce. Throughout, the host references established techniques (Cook’s Illustrated) and Steve Dunn’s gravy method, and ends with tasting notes and prompts to apply the concept to other dishes.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: The Foolproof Formula for Braising Beef (Catalan-Style Beef Stew) - Lan Lam
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: This video presents a practical, four-part braising formula illustrated through a Catalan-style beef stew. Lan Lam demonstrates selecting a tough-cut (boneless short ribs), trimming fat, and cutting meat into 2-inch pieces before browning to form a deep fond. The braising liquid is built with aromatics (tomato, bay leaf, smoked paprika) and a liquid mix of water and wine, plus thyme and cinnamon, then the meat is braised in the oven at a low, steady simmer. The lesson emphasizes testing doneness by texture rather than relying solely on a thermometer, explains collagen breakdown as the driver of tenderness, and shows finishing the sauce with defatting, reduction, and a picata (toasted almond, bread, garlic, parsley) blend, optionally with sautéed oyster mushrooms, and final seasoning adjustments for balance. The video also contrasts oven braising as more foolproof than stovetop braising and reinforces the core idea: start with a tough cut, develop a flavorful braising liquid, cook until tender, and finish with a sauce that clings to the meat.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Side Fond: Bonus Flavor from the Sides of the Pot (Pork Ragù with Pappardelle)
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: The video explains side fond, a flavor-building technique where browning and the Maillard reaction create flavorful browned bits on the sides of a pot. The host demonstrates how to set up ingredients (pancetta, pork shoulder, onion, fennel) and heat conditions to foster fond formation, then uses water and cream to dissolve and carry that fond into a braise. A 90-minute braise yields a juicy pork butt, and steam-condensation is used to scrape the fond off the sides without washing it away. The result is a richer sauce for ragù bianco with pappardelle, achieved without an extra searing step. The lesson covers when to add aromatics, the role of fat and collagen in tenderness, and why side fond can deepen flavor more efficiently by leveraging the pot’s side surface area.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Master Bacon: Skillet Rendering, Water-Assisted Cooking, and Oven Batch Method (Techniquely with Lan Lam)
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: America’s Test Kitchen’s Techniquely episode with Lan Lam compares classic skillet bacon with a water-assisted approach and an oven-based batch method, aiming for more consistent texture. The video walks through rendering fat in a 12-inch skillet without preheating, then introduces a water technique (quarter-cup for six slices) to control browning and reduce flipping, followed by a full-batch skillet method using water (one cup) and two-layer arrangement. It then demonstrates oven-baking bacon on a sheet pan at 400°F for larger quantities, and ends with explanations of common packaging terms (center-cut, non-nitrite/uncured, thick-cut) and practical serving tips. The transcript provides time-stamped steps, cues for doneness (bubble size and sizzle), and tips on draining and texture, all anchored by concrete timings and measurements from the demonstrations (e.g., 12-inch skillet, one cup water for a full package, 400°F oven).

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Myosin-Driven Textures: Burgers, Sausage, and Lion's Head Meatballs
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: This ATK Technique video explains how myosin development in ground meat governs texture across burgers, bulk sausage, and meatballs. It contrasts store-bought, highly processed grind with home-style grinding and mixing, showing deliberate controls to limit or maximize myosin release. The host demonstrates burger prep with four small-grind batches, minimal handling, and a brief pre-freeze to set texture, then sears and oven-finishes to a precise internal temperature. The sausage segment covers brining with salt, baking-soda–assisted myosin development, and a stand mixer approach for thorough mixing. The lion’s head meatballs illustrate maximal myosin development, including salt, baking soda, water, and a mixer-assisted blend, followed by long simmering in broth to exploit myosin’s emulsifying role. Throughout, the program reinforces that myosin can both bind water and fat for tenderness and act as a binding agent that can cause toughness if overdeveloped, guiding practical techniques for tender, juicy results in different ground-meat applications.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Three Rules for Better Simple Sandwiches (Pan Bagnat Demonstration)
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: This video reframes everyday, simple sandwiches as a trio of guiding concepts—bread treatment, flavor and texture contrast, and thoughtful assembly—then demonstrates how to apply them through a pan Bagnat-inspired tuna sandwich. It covers practical bread prep (toasting, optional interior removal to create a bread trough, and oiling), building a richly seasoned olive salad with tuna, tomatoes, and hard-cooked eggs, and the importance of pressing a filled sandwich to hold its shape. The host extends the lessons with two additional builds (turkey on ciabatta with kimchi and avocado; egg salad on rye with radishes and pickles) to illustrate how bread choice, fillings, and contrasts influence results. The video also provides appendices on make-ahead components (pickled avocado, Dijonnaise, sumac onions) and assembly tactics to prevent sogginess or fillings from slipping, capped with a sponge-based demonstration of waterproofing bread. Across sections, the content emphasizes planning, texture/flavor balance, and deliberate layering to improve even simple sandwiches.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Cold-Sear: A Fast, Dry-Heat Steak Sear Demonstration (Lan Lam, Techniquely)
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: The video compares multiple steak-cooking philosophies, foregrounding a fast, low-mess method called cold-searing while also explaining traditional pan-sear, oven-finish, reverse-sear, and sous-vide approaches. Lan Lam contrasts the outcomes (edge-to-edge doneness with a rosy center vs. a gray ring) and details a step-by-step cold-sear process using a dry, hot non-stick skillet, a thick boneless steak, and careful heat management. Key practices include drying the surface, peppering before searing, avoiding pre-salt, heating to drive off surface moisture, flipping every two minutes to build multiple brown layers, reducing heat to finish cooking toward a 125°F center, a five-minute rest, and finishing with coarse salt for texture. The video also outlines the advantages and downsides of each method and notes how sous-vide and reverse-sear compare in precision and equipment needs.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: How to "Dry Age" a Steak in Two Hours | Techniquely with Lan Lam
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: Lan Lam presents a home method to emulate dry-aged beef flavors in a matter of hours using shiokoji (koji) as a fermentation-inspired marinade on flank steak. The video opens with an overview of why dry-aged beef is prized—tenderness and intensified flavor with pronounced umami—then explains the enzymatic changes that occur during traditional aging. It introduces koji-based shiokoji and its enzymes (proteases, amylases, lipases), demonstrates selecting and preparing a steak (notably flank with silver skin removed), and shows coating the meat with shiokoji and refrigerating for 2–24 hours. After aging, the steak is cooked with a reverse-sear: a 300°F oven finish to about 130–135°F, followed by a quick skillet sear. The serving ideas include shiokoji compound butter, lemon, and flake salt. The video also touches on flavor variations and practical considerations for home cooks, including cost and practicality in lieu of traditional dry-aging.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: You Need to Let Your Food Stick: How and When Sticking Can Build Flavor, Texture, and Structure
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: America’s Test Kitchen host Lan Lam reframes the common assumption that sticking is universally bad by explaining how and why food sticks, when sticking is advantageous, and how cooks can control sticking with barriers, pan choice, and technique. The video covers (a) the mechanics of sticking at the protein–pan interface, (b) barrier strategies such as oil films and patinas on cast iron, (c) practical demonstrations including oven-baked French toast on a sprayed sheet, (d) the role of surfactant-containing cooking sprays to form thin, even barriers, (e) the use of fond to build pan sauces, and (f) specific demonstrations of sticking to shape texture—smashed burgers with lacy edges and a chiffon-based ice cream cake where sticking helps structure. The overarching message is balanced: don’t fear sticking in all cases, but recognize when it serves flavor, appearance, and ease of cooking, and when it should be minimized for cleanup or even browning objectives.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Glazes That Stick: two-coat technique and thick, clingy glazes for meat and fish
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: This ATK-Techniquely episode dissects glazes designed to stay put on proteins, showing how to build thick, clingy glazes that don’t melt away under heat. The host demonstrates a ketchup-based glaze for meatloaf and then pivots to two distinctive glaze approaches for pork chops and salmon: a gochujang–miso-based glaze for pork with a gentle cooking method, and a cornstarch-thickened salmon glaze built from a bold blend of vinegar, maple, soy, and liquid smoke. Key concepts include achieving a glossy, lacquer-like finish, the advantage of applying glaze in two coats, cooking meat at lower temperatures to preserve juiciness, and practical steps to prevent glaze from sliding off (half-coat first, avoid cross-contamination, broil for color). The episode also points viewers to additional salmon glazes and related recipes on AmericasTestKitchen.com and the ATK app.

video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.title: Pan Sauces Demystified: Easy Vinegar-Pepper and Red-Wine Variants
video-techniquely-with-lan-lam-america-s.summary: America's Test Kitchen presents a practical, technique-driven tour of pan sauces built from the fond left in the pan after searing protein. The video compares an easy flour-based version (using shallots, a touch of flour, chicken stock and pickle brine) with a more traditional red-wine pan sauce, and then highlights a butter-only finishing approach. Core concepts include: how to prepare and rest protein so the pan remains ready for sauce, how to deglaze and reduce to liberate fond, emulsifying cold butter into hot sauce to finish with richness, and recognizing when a sauce might break and how to rescue it.
